# Determination Has a ZIP Code in Your Brain — and Chronic Anxiety Is Its Neighbor

A nine-year-old boy with a brain tumor fired his family therapist, directed his own treatment through visualization and peer support, and survived. A Stanford research team accidentally discovered that the feeling driving that kind of behavior — not fear, not dread, but the specific positive urge to *push harder and keep going* — can be located in a single anatomical node inside the brain. Move the electrode a few millimeters in any direction, and the feeling disappears entirely.

These two facts, one clinical and one neuroscientific, turn out to be about the same thing. And for anyone working with family systems — whether as a therapist, a researcher, or someone trying to change their own patterns — the implications are worth sitting with carefully.

In a February 2022 lecture, psychiatrist and Bowen Theory scholar Dr. Michael Kerr drew a direct line between this neuroscience research and the work of differentiation of self. His conclusion was straightforward: sustained change requires determination, chronic anxiety continuously activates the same brain network around threat-monitoring, and the two are in direct competition with each other. Understanding that competition may be one of the most practically useful things a person working in family systems can do.

---

## The Accidental Discovery: Where Determination Lives in the Brain

The finding came from a clinical procedure, not a planned experiment. A team of neurologists at Stanford was implanting electrodes in a patient's brain as part of a standard clinical assessment. During one of the implantation cycles, they asked the patient to describe his sensations, thoughts, and feelings as the electrode was positioned in a specific location.

The patient did not report pain. He did not report fear or dread. He reported *determination* — a positive feeling, he said, that told him to push harder, to keep going, to get through whatever was in front of him.

The doctors moved the electrode a few millimeters in one direction. The feeling vanished. They moved it back. It returned. They located the same node in a second patient and found it in the same anatomical position.

What they had stumbled onto was a single tiny node within what neuroscientists call the emotional salience network — the brain system that monitors internal emotional states and the external environment, identifies what matters most among all incoming signals, and spurs the organism to act or not act accordingly. This network sits in close anatomical relationship with the executive control network, which keeps attention focused on goals and marshals the brain's resources once the salience network has flagged something as important.

Kerr described the researchers' conclusion this way: they had activated a kind of "grit switch" inside the emotional salience and executive control complex. The feeling of determination, it turns out, is not a vague motivational state. It has a location. It is produced by specific neurons. And it is reproducible.

---

## Why This Matters for Family Systems Work

Kerr made the bridge explicit. "It takes a determination to change," he said, connecting the electrode finding directly to the work of differentiation of self — the lifelong effort, central to Bowen Family Systems Theory, to develop a more clearly defined sense of self within one's emotional system while remaining in genuine contact with others.

Differentiation work is not primarily intellectual. It requires a person to stay present in emotionally activating relationships, to resist the pull toward automatic, anxiety-driven responses, and to act from a more considered position rather than a reactive one. Anyone who has tried this seriously knows that it is metabolically and emotionally costly in a way that is difficult to explain to someone who hasn't.

The neuroscience gives that cost a clearer shape. The emotional salience network — the same network that contains the determination node — is also the network that chronic anxiety never stops activating.

This is not a coincidence. It is a competition.

---

## Chronic Anxiety as a Continuous Drain on the Determination Circuit

During the Q&A following Kerr's lecture, several participants offered formulations that, taken together, build a remarkably complete picture of how chronic anxiety interferes with the kind of sustained effort differentiation requires.

Therapist Amy Post offered the most direct formulation. She proposed that the degree to which life energy is going into maintaining what she called "state-holding" — the organism's effort to preserve homeostatic stability, to keep the emotional system in its familiar equilibrium — is energy that is not available for determination. The chronic anxiety that lives in a family system, she suggested, functions as a latent pull back toward that prior state, continuously drawing on the same neural resources that determination requires.

Kerr found the formulation worth sitting with. "I'll keep thinking about that one," he said.

Dave Galloway offered a complementary account from his own experience. He described chronic anxiety not as a feeling of dread but as a continuous background state of vigilance — a scanning process, largely below conscious awareness, oriented around a single question: *What does the other person want?* This vigilance, he explained, was adaptive to the emotional programming of his family of origin. It was tuned to that system. But it runs constantly, generating a low-level anxiousness that then produces soothing behaviors — over-functioning, seeking the right answer, trying to please — that temporarily reduce the discomfort without resolving the underlying state.

Kerr connected this to the homeostasis framework: a disturbance in homeostasis activates the stress response, the stress response becomes chronic, and that chronic state is experienced as chronic anxiety within the individual. The stress response, he said, is central to understanding what is happening in the body as a whole.

Kathy Kerr added a further distinction. Acute anxiety, she noted, is adaptive — no one gets through a day without it. But chronic anxiety, especially when it pushes organisms to regress toward previous states that are not adaptive to their current situation, raises a harder question: what is its adaptive value? The answer she and Kerr arrived at together was that regression can sometimes motivate a call for action — but only when the pressure becomes severe enough to force a genuine break from the old pattern. Kerr cited Murray Bowen's observation that families dealing with schizophrenia often didn't change until their backs were literally against the wall, financial and emotional resources exhausted, and someone finally said: *I cannot keep doing this this way.*

The determination node, in that framing, is what gets activated when the wall is finally reached.

---

## Cancer Survivors, Nine-Year-Olds, and the Evidence for Determination

Two threads in the Q&A pushed the determination finding beyond the clinical and into something more vivid.

Lana Hardy raised the connection to cancer survival research. Kerr described a study in which a researcher examined a hospital's cancer registry, identified patients who had survived against the odds, and tried to determine what distinguished them from those who had not. The answer that emerged was not a specific treatment protocol or a particular drug regimen. It was determination — but determination expressed in two completely opposite directions. One patient told the doctor: *Throw everything you've got at me. I'm determined to get the best treatment available.* Another patient said: *If I stay in this hospital any longer, you're going to kill me. I'm determined to get out of here.* The common denominator was not the direction of the choice. It was the quality of the commitment behind it.

Janice Norton brought the final piece. She described a short paperback called *I Choose Life*, written by a therapist and a nine-year-old boy named Garrett Porter who survived an astrocytoma brain tumor that was, by medical expectation, going to kill him. The boy used visualization. He relied on a network of adults and friends for support. And at a certain point, he told his parents to keep going to family therapy — and stopped attending himself. He had decided he had had enough of that particular form of help, and he redirected his energy accordingly.

"The determination thing really comes through," Norton said.

Kerr's response was quiet but pointed. The book's title, he noted, is itself a statement of the determination node firing: *I choose life.* Not *I hope to survive.* Not *I am afraid of dying.* A choice. An active, forward-directed commitment to a specific outcome, sustained over time against significant opposition.

Neuroscience now has a name for what that nine-year-old was running on. And a location for it in the brain.

---

## What This Means in Practice

The picture that emerges from Kerr's lecture, the electrode study, and the Q&A discussion is not comfortable, but it is clarifying.

Differentiation of self — the central developmental task in Bowen Family Systems Theory — requires sustained determination. That determination is produced by a specific node in the emotional salience network. Chronic anxiety, which is the accumulated residue of a family system's multigenerational emotional programming, continuously activates the same network around threat-monitoring and state-holding. The two processes are not simply in tension. They are competing for the same neural real estate.

This means that the cost of differentiation work is not primarily intellectual. It is not a matter of learning the right concepts or understanding the theory clearly enough. It is a matter of having enough determination available — enough activation of that specific node — to sustain forward movement in the face of a system that is continuously pulling toward the familiar equilibrium.

It also means that chronic anxiety is not simply a symptom to be managed. It is, in a neurological sense, determination's most direct competitor. Understanding that competition — naming it, tracking it, working with it rather than around it — may be one of the most practically useful contributions neuroscience has yet made to family systems thinking.

---

## Key Takeaways

- A Stanford research team accidentally discovered that determination — the specific positive urge to persevere — is locatable in a single anatomical node of the emotional salience network, reproducible across patients, and eliminated by moving the electrode a few millimeters in any direction.
- Chronic anxiety continuously activates the same salience network around threat-monitoring and state-holding, making it determination's most direct neural competitor and helping explain why sustained differentiation work is so metabolically and emotionally costly.
- Evidence from cancer survivor research and clinical accounts — including a nine-year-old who directed his own treatment and survived a brain tumor — suggests that the direction of determined action matters less than the quality of commitment behind it; determination toward opposite choices can produce the same survival outcome.

---

## Glossary of Terms

- **Differentiation of self:** In Bowen Family Systems Theory, the lifelong process of developing a more clearly defined sense of self within one's emotional system while remaining in genuine contact with others, rather than either fusing with or cutting off from significant relationships.
- **Emotional salience network:** A brain system that monitors internal emotional states and the external environment, identifies the most relevant inputs among all incoming signals, and spurs the organism to act or not act accordingly; the network within which the determination node was located.
- **Executive control network:** A brain system that keeps attention focused on goals relevant to the organism and marshals neural resources once the salience network has flagged something as important; works in close coordination with the salience network.
- **Chronic anxiety:** In Bowen Theory, a sustained background level of anxiety that reflects the accumulated emotional programming of a multigenerational family system, distinct from acute anxiety, which is adaptive and time-limited.
- **State-holding:** A term used in the lecture to describe the organism's ongoing effort to preserve homeostatic stability — to keep the emotional system in its familiar equilibrium — which competes with the energy available for forward-directed determination.
- **Core affect:** A neurological state in higher animals that acts as a sentinel to watch for threats to homeostasis and influences an organism to respond accordingly; described as the input of the body combined with situational context and background knowledge to produce experienced emotions.
- **Homeostasis:** The ability of an organism or individual cell to maintain stable internal order even in the face of environmental changes that could threaten it; disruptions to homeostasis activate the stress response, which can become chronic and be experienced as chronic anxiety.
